title: GOD TOLD MOSES, “YOU CANNOT SEE MY FACE AND LIVE.” BUT THEN JESUS CAME—AND EVERYTHING CHANGED.
paragraphs: GOD TOLD MOSES, “YOU CANNOT SEE MY FACE AND LIVE.” BUT THEN JESUS CAME—AND EVERYTHING CHANGED.
The terrifying mystery of Exodus 33:18–23, the glory no human could endure, and the breathtaking reason sinners can now approach the God whose holiness once made even Moses hide.
There is something terrifying about the thought of standing before God.

Not the version of God we sometimes create in our imagination. Not a distant grandfather in heaven who smiles at everything and never confronts anything. Not a religious symbol we bring out on Sundays and quietly put away when Monday comes.
The living God.
The One who spoke light into existence before there was a sun.
The One before whom angels cover their faces.
The One who knows every thought you have ever buried, every sin you have ever justified, every tear you have ever hidden, and every secret you have convinced yourself nobody will discover.
Imagine standing before Him.
No church clothes to make you appear respectable. No carefully chosen words. No reputation to protect you. No one to impress.
Just you.
And the God who knows everything.
Now imagine asking that God to show you His glory.
That is exactly what Moses did.
And the answer he received should make every human being stop and think.
“Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live.” — Exodus 33:20 (KJV)
Read that again.
God did not say Moses was too sinful to be loved.
He did not say Moses was too insignificant to be noticed.
He said Moses could not see His face and live.
But here is the question that changes everything.
If even Moses—the man who spoke with God, led Israel out of Egypt, and stood on holy ground—could not endure the unveiled glory of God...
How can someone like you or me ever hope to stand in His presence?
And why does the New Testament tell us that one day we will see His face?
The answer begins in a mountain cleft, passes through a bloodstained cross, and ends with a promise so astonishing that even the most broken sinner has reason to hope.
But to understand it, we must return to the moment Moses made the boldest request of his life.
Israel had just committed an astonishing betrayal.
The people whom God had delivered from slavery had fashioned a golden calf and worshiped it. While Moses was receiving God's covenant instructions, the nation was bowing before an idol.
Think about that.
They had watched the Red Sea open.
They had eaten bread from heaven.
They had witnessed the mountain trembling beneath the presence of God.
And still, they turned away.
It is easy to shake our heads at Israel.
Until we remember how often we have done something painfully similar.
God answers a prayer, and we forget Him when life becomes comfortable.
God rescues us from a destructive season, and we slowly return to the very things that wounded us.
We sing about surrender on Sunday, then spend the rest of the week negotiating how much of our lives we are willing to give Him.
The golden calf may look different today.
Sometimes it is money.
Sometimes approval.
Sometimes a relationship we are terrified to lose.
Sometimes it is the version of ourselves we refuse to surrender.
And sometimes the idol is not something obviously wicked.
It is something good that has quietly become more important to us than God.
Israel's sin threatened the covenant relationship they had been called to enjoy. God spoke of judgment, and Moses interceded for the people.
Then came an extraordinary conversation.
Moses pleaded for God's presence to remain with Israel.
He understood something many of us spend our lives learning.
A promised land without the presence of God is not enough.
Success without Him is not enough.
Religious activity without Him is not enough.
And after God promised His presence, Moses made a request that seems almost impossible to comprehend.
“I beseech thee, shew me thy glory.” — Exodus 33:18 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the request reads:
הַרְאֵנִי נָא אֶת־כְּבֹדֶךָ
Har'ēnî nāʾ ʾet-kevōdekā.
“Please, show me Your glory.”
The Hebrew word kavod (כָּבוֹד) carries associations of weight, honor, and glory. In this passage, Moses is asking for a revelation of God's divine majesty.
He was not merely asking to see something beautiful.
He wanted to know God more deeply.
And God answered him in a way that reveals something essential about divine glory.
“I will make all my goodness pass before thee, and I will proclaim the name of the LORD before thee.” — Exodus 33:19 (KJV)
Do not miss that.
Moses asked to see glory.
God promised to reveal His goodness and proclaim His name.
God's glory is not merely overwhelming brightness or unimaginable power. His glory also includes the revelation of His holy character.
His goodness.
His mercy.
His righteousness.
His sovereign grace.
The God who is infinitely powerful is also the God who reveals Himself as merciful.
And yet, immediately after promising this revelation, God declared that Moses could not see His face and live.
Why?
Because the God Moses longed to see is not merely a greater version of ourselves.
He is the Creator.
We are creatures.
He is eternal.
We are finite.
He is perfectly holy.
We are fallen.
The Hebrew word for face, panim (פָּנִים), can refer to someone's literal face, but it also appears in expressions involving presence and personal encounter.
This matters because Exodus itself says that the LORD spoke to Moses “face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend” (Exodus 33:11).
Is the Bible contradicting itself?
Not at all.
The expression in verse 11 describes the remarkable directness and intimacy of God's communication with Moses. It does not mean Moses had already seen God's unveiled divine essence.
In verse 20, God places a limit on what Moses can behold.
Moses could truly know God without being able to comprehend or endure the fullness of His glory.
And that distinction matters.
Because intimacy with God does not make God less holy.
Grace does not make His glory less overwhelming.
And being loved by God does not mean we can approach Him on whatever terms we choose.
God is not dangerous because He is evil.
He is holy.
His glory is not something a mortal human can casually possess, control, or endure.
Scripture does not explain the physical mechanism by which seeing God's unveiled face would bring death. The passage establishes the reality of human limitation before divine glory.
Even Moses needed God to determine how much could be revealed.
Then something extraordinary happened.
God did not simply reject Moses' request.
He made provision for Moses to receive a genuine, yet limited, revelation of His glory.
“Behold, there is a place by me, and thou shalt stand upon a rock.” — Exodus 33:21 (KJV)
A place.
A rock.
A cleft.
And the protecting hand of God.
“And it shall come to pass, while my glory passeth by, that I will put thee in a clift of the rock, and will cover thee with my hand while I pass by.” — Exodus 33:22 (KJV)
Picture the scene.
Moses stands on the mountain.
He has asked for more of God than any human being could simply demand.
And the Lord Himself provides the protection necessary for the encounter.
Moses does not construct a shelter strong enough to withstand divine glory.
He does not earn immunity through years of obedience.
He does not become less human through religious achievement.
God provides the place.
God provides the covering.
God determines the revelation.
And Moses receives what God graciously allows him to see.
When the Lord says Moses will see His “back” but not His “face” (Exodus 33:23), we must be careful not to force a human body onto the invisible God.

The Hebrew word achor (אָחוֹר) can refer to what is behind or the back. In this extraordinary encounter, the language communicates a partial revelation rather than the full, direct sight Moses requested.
The passage uses humanly understandable language to describe a divine encounter beyond ordinary human experience.
And the central truth is breathtaking.
Moses could only behold what God revealed, in the way God permitted, under the protection God provided.
But there is something even more beautiful.
When God later passed before Moses in Exodus 34:6–7, He proclaimed His name and character.
“The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth...” (Exodus 34:6, KJV).
The revelation included mercy, patience, covenant faithfulness, forgiveness, and justice.
God was showing Moses that His glory cannot be separated from who He is.
He is not only the God whose holiness exposes sin.
He is also the God who is merciful and gracious.
But He does not pretend guilt is innocence.
And here is where the story begins to reach into our own lives.
Because many of us want the mercy of God without the holiness of God.
We want forgiveness without repentance.
Peace without surrender.
Heaven without transformation.
A Savior who comforts us, but never confronts the things destroying us.
Yet the God who revealed His goodness to Moses is the same God who takes sin seriously.
And perhaps that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
It forces us to ask whether we truly want God...
Or merely the benefits of having Him near.
Have you ever prayed for God to change your circumstances while quietly resisting His desire to change your heart?
Have you ever asked Him for peace while holding on to the very sin that has been stealing it?
Have you ever wanted to feel His presence without wanting to obey His Word?
Those questions are not meant to drive you into hopelessness.
They are meant to lead you into the light.
Because the greatest surprise in this story is not that Moses could not see God's face.
It is that the holy God was willing to reveal Himself to Moses at all.
And centuries later, that willingness would become visible in a way Moses could scarcely have imagined.
A child was born in Bethlehem.
Not surrounded by the thunder of Sinai.
Not accompanied by an army of earthly kings.
Not arriving in the kind of power the world expects.
He came in humility.
And His name was Jesus.
The apostle John wrote something that should stop us in our tracks.
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.” — John 1:14 (KJV)
The Greek reads:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Not merely appeared to be human.
Not simply sent a message through a prophet.
The eternal Word became flesh.
The Son of God entered human history.
And John says, “We beheld his glory.”
Think about the contrast.
Moses pleaded, “Show me Your glory.”
John declares, “We beheld his glory.”
But we must understand this correctly.
Jesus did not cease to be divine when He became human.
Nor did His incarnation mean that every person who looked at His human face automatically saw the unveiled divine essence that Moses was forbidden to behold.
The Son truly became man while remaining truly God.
His glory was revealed through His person, His words, His works, His obedience, and ultimately His death and resurrection.
And the New Testament goes even further.
“For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” — 2 Corinthians 4:6 (KJV)
Read those final words slowly.
“In the face of Jesus Christ.”
The glory of God.
The face of Jesus Christ.
The God who told Moses that no mortal could behold His unveiled face now makes His glory known through His incarnate Son.
Not because God's holiness has diminished.
Not because sin has become harmless.
But because Jesus Christ is the perfect revelation of the Father.
Jesus Himself said:
“He that hath seen me hath seen the Father.” — John 14:9 (KJV)
He was not saying that the Father and Son are the same person.
He was revealing the perfect unity of the Son with the Father and the truth that to know the Son is to know the Father whom He reveals.
And then comes the part of the Gospel that should bring us to our knees.
The One who revealed divine glory allowed sinful human beings to mock Him.
The One through whom all things were created permitted soldiers to strike Him.
The One who was worthy of worship was crowned with thorns.
The One who had never sinned was condemned as a criminal.
And the hands that healed the sick were nailed to a cross.
Can you feel the weight of that?
The God whose holiness Moses could not fully behold had come near in the person of His Son.
And humanity responded by crucifying Him.
Yet even that terrible act did not defeat the saving purpose of God.
At the cross, the sinless Christ willingly bore the penalty of sin for His people.
He did not become sinful in His own character.
He remained the righteous One.
But He suffered for the unrighteous to bring us to God.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” — 1 Peter 3:18 (KJV)
There it is.
The answer to the question that has haunted this story from the beginning.
How can sinful people ever come into the presence of a holy God?
Not by pretending they are righteous.
Not by collecting enough religious achievements.
Not by giving enough money.
Not by hiding the worst parts of their past.
Through Jesus Christ.
Through His atoning death.
Through His resurrection.
Through His grace received by faith.
Through the righteousness of Christ, not our own.
Moses needed God's gracious protection to receive a limited revelation of glory.
We need the saving work of Jesus Christ to be reconciled to God.

These are not identical events, and Exodus 33 does not explicitly identify the cleft of the rock as Jesus. Yet the scene beautifully illustrates a truth fulfilled in the Gospel: access to the holy God is possible only because God graciously makes a way.
And that way is not a location on a mountain.
It is a Person.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6 (KJV)
Maybe you are reading this with a past you wish you could erase.
Maybe people know the scandal but not the suffering behind it.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove that you are not the person you used to be.
Maybe you are still struggling with something you promised God you would never return to.
Or perhaps you look perfectly fine to everyone around you.
You serve.
You smile.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say amen.
But there are nights when you sit alone and wonder whether God is tired of you.
Whether you have failed too many times.
Whether forgiveness still reaches someone who knew better and sinned anyway.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
It says Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide your darkness.
It calls you to bring it into the light.
The Gospel does not promise that repentance will never hurt.
It promises that those who come to Christ in faith will not be cast out.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
You do not have to clean up your entire life before coming to the Savior.
But you cannot sincerely come to Him while insisting that He has no right to change you.
His grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
It is the beginning of a new life.
Repentance is not the price you pay to purchase God's love.
It is the Godward turning that accompanies genuine faith.
And real faith does not merely admire Jesus from a distance.
It trusts Him.
It receives Him.
It follows Him.
Sometimes stumbling.
Sometimes weeping.
Sometimes learning through painful correction.
But never beyond the reach of His faithful grace.
Perhaps this is the moment to stop pretending.
Not before strangers.
Not for the approval of a religious crowd.
But before the Lord who already knows the truth.
Tell Him where you are struggling.
Confess the sin you have been defending.
Bring Him the shame you have been carrying.
Ask Him to renew your heart.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic spiritual experience.
You need the Savior.
Not because typing those words earns forgiveness.
But because sometimes a simple, honest response can become the beginning of a deeper conversation, a request for prayer, or a testimony that helps someone else stop hiding.
And if you are not comfortable sharing publicly, bring those words to God in private. He hears you there, too.
Now return to Moses for a moment.
He wanted to see God's glory.
He was given a glimpse.
But the Bible does not end with a glimpse.
It ends with a promise.
In Revelation 22, the apostle John describes the final dwelling of God's redeemed people.
There is no curse.
The throne of God and of the Lamb is there.
His servants worship Him.
And then comes one of the most extraordinary statements in all of Scripture.
“And they shall see his face; and his name shall be in their foreheads.” — Revelation 22:4 (KJV)
Did you catch it?
In Exodus, Moses was told he could not see God's face and live.
In Revelation, God's redeemed servants will see His face.
How can both be true?
Because Scripture is not describing the same condition of humanity in both scenes.
In Exodus, Moses is a mortal man receiving a limited revelation of divine glory.
In Revelation, God's people have been brought into their final, redeemed condition in the new creation.
Sin and the curse are gone.
Death has been defeated.
The redeemed belong fully to God.
And the promise of seeing His face is no longer beyond their capacity.
The apostle John also writes:
This does not mean believers become gods or cease to be creatures.
It means that when Christ appears, His people will be transformed into the likeness appropriate to their glorified life with Him.
What was impossible for mortal humanity in Exodus becomes the promised joy of redeemed humanity in the new creation.
Not because human beings finally make themselves worthy.
But because Jesus saves completely.
The cross was not an emergency plan.
The resurrection was not an unexpected recovery.
And heaven is not a reward for people who managed to be impressive enough.
Salvation is the work of God's grace in Jesus Christ.
From beginning to end.
And one day, those who belong to Christ will see Him.
Not through the uncertainty of earthly circumstances.
Not through the tears of unanswered questions.
Not through the dimness of our present understanding.
But in the joy of His unveiled presence, as Scripture promises.
Imagine that.
The believer who spent years fighting addiction, finally free from every sinful desire.
The mother who cried over her wandering child, standing in a world where sorrow has ended.
The person who carried shame for decades, now fully restored in the presence of the Savior.
The exhausted disciple who kept trusting Jesus through suffering, finally seeing the One who sustained them.
No more curse.
No more death.
No more sin.
No more hiding.
And no fear that the glory of God will destroy those whom Christ has redeemed.
Only the fullness of life with Him.
That is why the Gospel is so much greater than motivational religion.
It does not simply promise to improve your week.
It announces that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death and opened the way to eternal life.
And it calls you to respond.
Not tomorrow, if your heart is being convicted today.
Not after you have exhausted every other solution.
Not after you have learned how to look spiritual.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His finished work.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him in repentance and faith.
And remember that your confidence rests not in the strength of your grip on Him, but in the faithfulness of the Savior who holds His people.
This is why we keep sharing the Gospel at Gospel Warrior.
Because somewhere tonight, a person is wondering whether their past has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Somewhere, a believer is quietly losing hope.
Somewhere, a family is praying for a prodigal to come home.
Somewhere, someone has never understood why Jesus had to die.
And somewhere, a person who has spent years running from God may be one Scripture-filled message away from seriously considering the claims of Christ.
We cannot manufacture conversion.
Only God can give new life.
But we can faithfully proclaim His Word.
We can encourage the weary.
We can speak truth to the confused.
We can remind the ashamed that the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him.
And you can be part of that work.
A simple share can place biblical truth before someone who would never think to search for a Christian message.
And if you have stayed with this message until now, I would love to hear something meaningful from you.
What speaks to your heart most: God's holiness, His mercy, or the promise that His redeemed people will one day see His face?
There is also a deeper way to help sustain this ministry.

Gospel Warrior is building and sharing resources for people who want more than occasional inspiration. We want to encourage serious engagement with Scripture, repentance, prayer, spiritual maturity, and a life increasingly shaped by Jesus Christ.
Our desire is to keep biblical learning accessible while continuing to develop and expand this work.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Not fear.
Not guilt.
But from a sincere desire to help make biblical encouragement and discipleship available to more people.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards, and no purchase can increase anyone's standing before God.
You are not less valuable because you cannot give financially.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Christ's grace cannot be purchased.
And God's love is not measured by a monthly payment.
What we are inviting you into is something much simpler and more beautiful.
A community that wants to take the Word of God seriously.
A ministry that desires to point people away from self-sufficiency and toward the sufficiency of Jesus.
A shared commitment to proclaiming the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners, restores broken lives, and makes all things new.
Because the real glory of this story is not Moses' courage.
It is God's mercy.
It is not our ability to climb high enough to reach heaven.
It is the grace of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
It is not the strength of our religious performance.
It is the finished work of the crucified and risen Lord.
Moses stood in the cleft of a rock because God graciously protected him.
We stand in hope because Jesus Christ has reconciled us to God.
And the final chapter of our story, for all who belong to Him, is not a closed door before divine glory.
It is the promise of seeing His face.
So when the enemy reminds you of your scandal, remember the Savior.
When shame reminds you of your failures, remember the cross.
When fear whispers that you will never change, remember the power of the resurrection.
And when this world leaves you longing for something it cannot give, remember the promise awaiting the redeemed.
One day, faith will give way to sight.
One day, the tears of God's people will be wiped away.
One day, the Savior whom we have loved without seeing will be revealed in glory.
And every believer who has been rescued by His grace will know that the greatest gift of salvation was never merely escaping judgment.
It was being brought home to God.
The face Moses could not behold in his mortal condition is the face God's redeemed people are promised they will one day see—and the only reason that hope exists is Jesus.
